speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I will begin by briefly touching on the history of the Legal Service.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It will give Members some context for the changes being proposed today.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The framework for the Legal Service was established via the 1959 Constitution, which marked Singapore’s transition to internal self-government.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Over the years, adjustments were made to the way the Legal Service was run.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But the fundamental structure remained unchanged for many decades, until two rounds of major changes.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Major changes were made to create a more systematic talent management system.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: There were two key changes to the Constitutional structure.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: First, the composition of the LSC was expanded.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Since independence, Members will note that the LSC had comprised the Chief Justice (CJ), the Attorney-General (AG), the Chairman of the Public Service Commission (Chairman/PSC), a Supreme Court Judge and two members of the PSC, as nominated by the Chairman/PSC.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Unlike today, all of the members of the LSC were members by virtue of some other office that they held separately.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The CJ, AG and Chairman/PSC would continue to be on the LSC.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But in addition, up to six additional members, who need not be Supreme Court Judges or PSC members, could be nominated by the Prime Minister, the CJ and the Chairman/PSC.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The rationale was to bring in members, including those from the private sector, with a wider range of experience, for example, in personnel management, or who have knowledge of the legal service or the legal profession.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: A second key change that was made then was to put in place a system of autonomous personnel boards (PBs), which would have charge over different classes of Legal Service Officers (LSOs).

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I will cover this in more detail later on in my speech.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: There was a significant shift in favour of specialisation, in response to the increasing scope and complexity of legal work.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Two separate career tracks were introduced for the LSOs in the middle ranks: the judicial and legal tracks.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: LSOs in the middle-ranks could elect to specialise along either track.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They could be posted to jobs within either the Judicial or the Legal Branch to build experience.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The PBs were also restructured along the Branch lines to oversee the career development pathways of the LSOs in the respective tracks.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The enduring challenge has been our very small pool of talent, due to our small size.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This has been the raison d’etre for keeping with an integrated model.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: LSOs could be deployed interchangeably across Judicial and Legal Branches over the course of their career.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This principle was, in fact, recognised very early on.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The 1955 Malayanisation Commission, which was set up to accelerate the pace of localising the public service, in preparation for self-government, recommended that Legal Service officers be transferred from the Judicial side to the Legal side and vice versa, so as to “give officers an all-round training, and also to overcome the present objection of potential recruits to having experience limited to one side of the Service only which leads to a monotonous and incomplete professional career.” It was also agreed that all-round experience was beneficial, and that it would be best for officers to have experience at the Bar, on the Bench, as well as in the Attorney-General’s Department.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It took 30 years for the Legal Service to grow to 235 LSOs in 1995.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This number grew significantly, to 589 LSOs in 2014.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But even then, a fully specialist service was not a viable option.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: There were only 159 officers in the Judicial Branch; and 419 officers in the Legal Branch.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: With these numbers, having specialist services would leave officers, on the judicial side especially, lacking in opportunities for growth and career development.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: An “incomplete professional career”, to quote the words of the Malayanisation Commission.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This would hamper the ability to attract and also retain talent.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The Legal Service has played a key role in the development of our legal system and, consequently, in building Singapore’s reputation for commitment to the rule of law.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As Former CJ Yong Pung How said previously: “... the Legal Service has played a very important role in the success which Singapore has achieved as a nation.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: LSOs in the Judicial Branch have contributed to building a world-class Judiciary that is both strong and trusted.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: LSOs in the Legal Branch, such as in the Attorney-General’s Chambers (AGC) and in the various Ministries, support effective and nimble functioning of the Executive and Parliament.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For example, officers in AGC's Legislative Division, not only draft all the laws that are tabled and debated in this House, and I am sure Members are very familiar with all the Bills that have come, sometimes at breakneck speed, but also many pieces of subsidiary legislation that are critical for the effective functioning of the Executive.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Our international lawyers, they defend Singapore’s interests on the global front and make an outsize contribution to the continued vitality of the rules-based international order.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The high levels of public trust in these institutions is also worth noting.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: On the world stage, in the Heritage Foundation’s 2021 Index of Economic Freedom, Singapore achieved the highest scores among 184 countries for judicial effectiveness.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The World Economic Forum placed Singapore first in its 2019 Global Competitiveness Index, in terms of the efficiency of its legal framework in settling disputes.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The COVID-19 pandemic that we have just been experiencing and we are still in, has shown the depth and excellence of our Legal Service.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: LSOs in both the Judicial and Legal branches have worked tremendously hard to deal with the challenges brought about by COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: LSOs in the Legal Branch provided crucial legal support to the Government response to the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In January 2020, AGC stood up a Cross-Divisional Task Force, staffed by LSOs from the AGC and the legal divisions in various Ministries to provide urgent cross-cutting advice to the Government on all areas of the national pandemic response.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For example, establishing Government quarantine facilities, contract tracing, border security, ensuring continued trade flows for essential goods and services and supplies, financing the various COVID-19 response budgets, and also vaccine procurement.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, it is not just the quality, but also the speed of the responses from our officers.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: LSOs, including drafters from AGC, worked closely with policy officers in many Ministries as well as with private sector representatives to roll out a series of urgent measures to mitigate the economic impact of the pandemic on individuals and businesses.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: These measures, which required major pieces of legislation to be drafted in record time, included, and I think Members will recall over the last 18 months: (a) temporary relief from contractual obligations, (b) a rental relief framework, done more than once; (c) simplified frameworks for financially distressed companies to liquidate their businesses or restructure their debts; and (d) a framework for the negotiation of contracts affected by the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The quickly drafted legislation also allowed the Government to quickly implement new measures to control the spread of the disease.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: When circuit breaker measures were imposed to stop the spread of the virus, LSOs in the Courts, AGC and MinLaw, with other officers in the various agencies, worked together to formulate legislation to ensure the continued and undisrupted access to justice in spite of the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The Courts operationalised a framework for remote hearings, developed a wide range of pandemic-related protocols.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This ensured continued, undisrupted access to justice, even in the middle of the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: To enforce the Infectious Diseases Act and COVID-19-related legislation, prosecutors worked closely with law enforcement agencies to assess the evidence and take quick action in all cases.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: On the international front, LSOs in the International Affairs Division ensured that our COVID-19 measures remained consistent with our international obligations.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As the situation improved in Singapore, they also assisted the Government in negotiating essential travel and air bubble arrangements to sustain economic exchanges and maintain our relevance as a regional and global hub.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, what I have just outlined has been the model that we have adopted since Singapore achieved self-government.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It has served us well to build up a Legal Service into the excellent institution that it is today and I think Members will agree that Singapore has benefited immensely.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Over the years, the Government has considered the question of whether an integrated or a specialist service would best serve Singapore's needs.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We recognise the pros and cons both ways.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The challenge has been and continues to be finding the right balance for our own circumstances, our own context and our needs.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As mentioned, the small talent pool has been a constraint and that is something that we keep in mind as we consider the options.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In July this year, Mr Murali Pillai, with the support of other Members, spoke on this matter in Parliament, calling on the Government to study the feasibility of setting up a separate JSC for judicial officers.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Several members spoke and made good points about the increasing need for specialisation, including for the Judiciary, given the increasing factual and legal complexities of the cases presented to Court.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Minister Shanmugam agreed with their observations that the benefits of specialisation are likely to continue to grow as the Legal Service continues growing and maturing as an institution.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As Minister Shanmugam has said recently, the amendment is a finely balanced one.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: You can make a good case for not changing now and waiting.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Although this is still a relatively small number in context, it will allow us to have specialist services whilst retaining the benefits of the integrated model through a system of secondments.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Officers today have many opportunities to gain meaningful exposure and develop their careers.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Since 2014, both the Judicial Branch and the Legal Branch have made various changes to deepen specialist skillsets.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: There has also been a significant emphasis on the training of our judges to develop specific competencies required for the judicial role.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In 2015, Members might recall the Singapore Judicial College was established as the central training body for the Judiciary.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The State Courts and the Family Courts also run their own training programmes to help their judicial officers develop both deeper subject-matter knowledge as well as the necessary practical skills.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: At AGC, the AGC Academy was set up to take charge of managing the training for AGC officers.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Competency frameworks were developed so that individual training roadmaps could be drawn for each officer according to their own area of practice and specific level of expertise.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The Academy also organises regular workshops and lectures by subject-matter experts in both core and developing areas of the law, for AGC officers.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Cross-departmental clusters and specialist tracks have been established to help build expertise in particular areas of law.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Each Commission will focus on the particular demands of their respective services.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They will have flexibility to adapt their personnel management and development frameworks according to their respective services' specific needs.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The shift to a specialist model is not so much to address the problems of today but really a matter of forward planning, preparing for the challenges of the future.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As Minister Shanmugam said in his response to Mr Murali's Motion, the key question is: when is the right time to move?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We could take a wait-and-see approach, given what I have said, and maintain the current system and make small adjustments at the margins, smaller tweaks; or we can make the move now, prepare ourselves for the future.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We believe this will, eventually, make sense: to split the two services when the Legal Service grows further.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Broadly, the new provisions seek to replicate the existing provisions in respect of the current LSC, with appropriate adjustments to be made where necessary in introducing the JSC.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It will consist of existing LSOs holding posts in the Supreme Court or a subordinate court.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: All other LSOs will remain in the reconstituted Legal Service.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Clause 14 inserts new articles to establish a JSC and to reconstitute the LSC.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The new Articles 111B to 111I relate to the new JSC while 111J to 111Q relate to the reconstituted LSC.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The composition of the Commissions is set out in the new Articles 111B and 111J of the Constitution.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Chairman/PSC will be the ex-officio Vice-President of both Commissions.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The key change here is the hardcoding of Chairman/PSC's role as Vice-President of both Commissions.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Other than this, the remaining provisions replicate the current position in the Constitution.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, the respective Presidents of the Commissions, Chairman/PSC and the Prime Minister may nominate up to two members, whose appointment is subject to a Presidential veto.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Where any of them nominate two members, then at least one of them must be legally trained and of adequate seniority in order for both to be appointed.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The existing disqualifications that you see today will continue to apply.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Similar to today, Personal Boards (PBs) may be established to exercise certain functions of the two Commissions.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: However, there will be some structural changes to the PBs, which I will take Members through.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In 2014, Members may recall that I had said PBs were restructured along Branch lines instead of by seniority.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This was part of a broader shift towards specialisation, as I mentioned earlier.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Officers at Superscale Grade 2 and above continue to be overseen by the LSC directly.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The two Boards also oversee career development pathways in the Legal and Judicial tracks.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Both are chaired by CJ, who is President of the LSC.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The Judicial Branch Special Personnel Board comprises CJ and three other Supreme Court Judges, and the Legal Branch Special Personnel Board comprises the CJ and senior members of the AGC, including the AG and a Supreme Court Judge.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As part of the review, we also reviewed the appropriate structure for the PBs in the context of the changes that we seek to make for the proposed specialist model.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: With the restructuring, we have decided, following discussions with both CJ and AG, to shift to a system of formalised delegation.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The structure of the Commissions already align authority and responsibility, reducing the need for devolution.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: CJ and AG, as Presidents of their respective Commissions, will be closely involved in the management of the officers in their respective Commissions.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They will each be able to nominate Supreme Court Judges and Deputy Attorneys-General to the Commission if they so choose.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Both offices are involved in the management of their organisations and enjoy constitutional protection for their independence.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: A system of formalised delegation will facilitate alignment of purpose and efficient decision-making and also facilitate the division of responsibilities between the Commissions and the PBs.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Under this proposed structure, Commissions will be empowered to delegate, by way of subsidiary legislation, stipulated functions and powers to one or more of the PBs.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: These are to be exercised under the Commission's direction and control.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In terms of composition of the PBs, the Articles set out a closed list of persons who may be appointed as PB members.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: There is also a requirement that PBs must have at least three members to ensure a diversity of voices within a PB and to bring balance to its discussion and decisions.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Safeguards, at the same time, will be retained.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As is the case today, these matters will be decided at the Commission level because matters relating to senior officers should be decided directly by the Commissions, and functions of discipline and dismissal have serious professional implications and consequences.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Cross-Service secondments will continue to be available on application after the restructuring.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I mentioned cross-Service secondments earlier in my speech.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Secondments will be available under a framework jointly developed by the two Commissions.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Such movements will likely be subject to the prevailing rules or requirements developed by the two Commissions; the needs of the Services, obviously, given their specific manpower needs, including the availability of positions; and, necessarily, the officers' relevant experience and suitability for the job.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: These clauses do not relate to the Commissions.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: These clauses amend the references in the Constitution to various statutes relating to Government borrowing.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The changes are consequential to the amendments made in the Government Borrowing (Miscellaneous Amendments) Bill, which was just debated.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In July, my fellow members from the Government Parliamentary Committee (GPC) for Law, Mr Murali Pillai, Mr Lim Biow Chuan and Mr Christopher de Souza had spoken about the need to consider whether it would be feasible to set up a separate Judicial Service Commission that would be in a better position to nurture specialist judicial officers.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The Government, in response, has stated that it will consider and study the proposals and, so, I am glad that these Bills have now come to be tabled before this House.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The integrated model of our Legal Service, where officers are deployed to both judicial and legal branches, has previously met our manpower needs and helped us to build up our dispute resolution hub and status as a well-respected judiciary in the world.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is no mean feat, particularly given our small population and limited talent pool.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We have heard from the Minister about the great work that our Legal Service Officers have done, especially to meet our COVID-19 pandemic challenges as well.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: But as Singapore adds to its repertoire of being the preferred international dispute hub, we need to ensure that our Judiciary and Legal Service are also well-equipped to meet any new challenges ahead.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In the midst of fast-paced disruptions to our legal environment and profession, we are also facing a real competition with other emerging and lucrative sectors to train and retain the talent pool both in our Singapore Bar, the legal service and our Bench.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In preparation to meet future challenges caused by these changes, we need to build a strong and deep bench, towards specialisation of emerging areas of law and expertise required in the future.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, we also need to ensure good range of exposure, especially for our younger officers.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In this regard, younger does not mean in terms of age but for those less experienced.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I do have some clarifications that I would like to cover in three parts: (a) firstly, the career in the Courts; (b) secondly, the challenges in the future; and (c) and the last part is the expertise in community-niche and culturally sensitive areas, which I will deliver in Malay.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For example, existing office holders in the Supreme Courts or other subordinate Courts, like the Family Justice Courts, shall come under the newly-formed Judicial Service Commission (JSC).

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: A "judicial branch officer" is defined as an existing officer who is holding a post in the Supreme Court or a Subordinate Court.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: My question is: what would be the definition of a "Subordinate Court", besides the Family Justice Courts and the State courts, what others can be taken into consideration?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We are also facing the challenge of a limited talent pool.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: They are either Senior Counsel or senior practitioners taken from the Bar, one of whom I have appeared before, he was my arbitrator, another was an opposing counsel, the third I have worked with.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As much as I am glad that we have very talented and esteemed appointments to the judiciary bench, the thinning of the talent at the Bar is a very real risk to our legal profession.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We need to ensure that the deep bench in our Courts does not come at the expense of the Bar and deplete our talent pool at the Singapore Bar which is detrimental to our status of our dispute resolution hub.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is so that they can get sufficient experience; and also be exposed to experience in the other courts.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Hence, I would like to ask whether there would be flexibility to allow for transfers between both commissions to better prepare ourselves for the future needs of the Bench.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Speaking about the future needs of the Bench, this flows into the second part of my speech on challenges in the future.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The future challenges of greater cross-border litigation which not only involve complex legal or factual issues but also inevitably involves issues of conflict of laws and interface between common law and civil law systems in the various legal systems in other countries.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: New and specialised areas of law, for example, those involving smart contracts and cryptocurrency, would also require our judges to be equipped with the necessary commercial and perhaps, private practice experience and practical know-how.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: These would greatly complement the technical and legal skills already on the Bench.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Ultimately, a strong Bench would help to attract more disputes and bolster our dispute resolution hub status as a nation.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We thus need judges who understand practice and commercial realities.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Thus, without the risk of thinning of the Bar, perhaps the Ministry could look into the secondment of Judicial Service officers in specific private practice areas or international postings in the early parts of their career.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Of course, this is subject to issues of conflict of interest in the future and disclosure of associations in the future, once that officer leaves private practice to rejoin the Judiciary.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, such declarations are already the norm now when judges declare any potential conflict of interest prior to being docketed as a judge for a case.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Already, we have seen in the courts how a docket system of specialist judges with the relevant practice experience and managing the case from the outset would improve the case management and our cases in litigation have now progressed efficiently and effectively.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Perhaps also to complement the skillset, we can have more invited International Judges (IJs) to be part of our Judiciary and not just for cases before the Singapore International Commercial Courts (SICC), but perhaps the IJs, or International Judges, can also sit in specific High Court cases or appeals whenever necessary.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We not only have to broaden our talent pool to meet future challenges, we would also have to deepen our expertise in certain niche areas where perhaps there would be some religious or cultural sensitivities.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In this regard, Mr Speaker, I will move on to the last part of my speech which I will deliver in Malay, on community, cultural and religious sensitivities.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In Malay):   To attract international funds or high net worth individuals to establish endowments or invest in Singapore, we must further strengthen Singapore's status as a leading dispute resolution hub.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In addition, the Islamic financial sector has seen an increase in cases filed in courts and arbitration processes around the world, including institutions in Malaysia and the Middle East.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: These cases require in-depth expertise and a comprehensive legal framework for handling Islamic financial dispute cases.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It also requires a prudent and sensitive approach tailored to each specific region.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Furthermore, our constitution recognises the special position of the Malays and outlines the Government's commitment to protect the interests of our Malay-Muslim community and our Malay language.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In terms of law, Muslim law forms part of the law of the land.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Thus, our civil courts have the power to interpret Muslim law itself.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It not only provides the necessary specialization, but also can balance the approach that needs to be taken in dealing with specific cases.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I understand that this is already happening, but perhaps the career path and development of the seconded JSC officers can be further clarified so that this rotation can attract more JSC officers.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I also recommend that cross-sharing and learning be established between courts, including Syariah Court and civil court officers and all training perhaps can be conducted under the auspices of the Singapore Judicial College.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In English): Mr Speaker, Sir, I support the Bill.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The Constitutional Amendment Bill and the Judicial Service (Miscellaneous Amendments) Bill before us today provide for the creation of a separate Judicial Service.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The call for a separate Judicial Service is not something new at all.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: There has been calls for separate Judicial Services over the past 35 years and indeed, from all sides of the House.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The Workers' Party former Secretary General and former Member for Anson, the late Mr J.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Jeyaretnam, called for a separate Judicial Service Commission back in 1986.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Former Nominated Member of Parliament and President of the Law Society, Mr Chandra Mohan K Nair, called for it in 2004.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In our manifesto for the 2011 General Election, the Workers' Party called for a separate Judicial Service.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The hon Mr Murali Pillai proposed a separate Judicial Service Commission in November 2020, and again, in the Adjournment Motion in July this year together with the hon Mr Lim Biow Chuan and Mr Christopher de Souza.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In November 2020, following the Ms Parti Liyani saga, my colleagues, the hon Member for Aljunied, Ms Sylvia Lim and Ms He Ting Ru, the hon Member for Seng Kang, filed a Motion named "Justice for All".

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In my speech in the "Justice for All" Motion, I said that it might still be worthwhile for the proposed review then, to still consider whether we should have a more specialised or dedicated Judicial track at the State Court level encompassing Magistrates and District Judges, continuing inter-services posting or rotation with other branches of the legal service, particularly with the Attorney-General's Chambers (AGC).

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Today, I am heartened to see the Government taking the first step to set up a Judicial Service separate from the current legal service.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Currently, the Chief Justice (CJ) is the president of the LSC and the Attorney-General (AG) and the Public Service Commission (PSC) Chairman sit on the commission together with two other members, each nominated by the Attorney-General, the PSC chairman and the Prime Minister.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I assume that the reconstituted rows in the respective commissions intend that the AG and CJ cannot be nominated by anyone to be members of the JSC and the LSC respectively.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: And if my assumption is wrong here, I am happy for the Minister to clarify, but this must surely be the case as this would promote independence between the two commissions.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: And in the case of the AG, not taking a role in a JSC, it would demonstrate greater judiciary independence.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In particular, it has always been well-regarded by many commercial lawyers elsewhere.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: As a shipping lawyer, I can further attest to that also, because the cross-border nature of our shipping legal work, both contentious and non-contentious, require us to work with lawyers from different maritime jurisdictions.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: And the issue of finding jurisdiction for both the contracts we draft and the cases we do, often has to do with finding strategic, reliable and reputable jurisdictions, which we can persuade our clients and other stakeholders to accept.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: With the new JSC being split from the current LSC, and the more dedicated judicial track, which must surely envisage more dedicated recruitment as well as Human Resources (HR) policies, even more attention to judicial training at all levels, especially lower to mid levels, as well as a more enhanced career progression plans for all judicial officers, it is hoped that the public will be able to see better access to justice, even better quality judgments at all levels, including the various tribunals, State Courts, the High Court and the Appellate Courts above, as well as the delivery of just outcomes for all litigants.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I believe that a separate JSC should be given optimum autonomy to plan its recruitment in human resource development, independent of the reconstituted LSC.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Having a separate JSC will, hopefully, allow it to look at recruitment, professional and continuing training and retention of personnel with a new focus as it strives to work towards building a team of officers who are specialists in being judicial officers, not merely Legal Service Officers.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I hope that with the JSC, our Courts can continue to recruit and develop more specialists in different areas, be it technology, construction, finance, IP, so on and so forth.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This should also not just be at the higher levels, such as in the High Court, but also in the State Courts.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This will enable our Courts to maintain its high standing among judiciaries all over the world.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: He or she must, of course, be learned in law, and also in the area of specialisation that he or she is known for, beyond pure commercial law and, particularly, in areas like criminal and family law.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The ability of judges to understand and empathise with the different challenges faced by litigants of different socioeconomic backgrounds is critical.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In my speech at that "Justice for All" Motion, I also said a specialised Judicial Service may be preferable to the current system to provide more distance between prosecutors and those working as magistrates and judges.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: For example, to avoid having AGC colleagues, some of them being more senior colleagues, arguing cases before them, knowing that they may be posted back to AGC again.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I had asked what safeguards will be in place to encourage reasonable distance.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This suggestion to set up the JSC is not mine alone.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Several hon Members made the same suggestion in this House, both before and after me, and we have just heard from the hon Member Mr Dennis Tan an account of the other Members who have spoken in this House asking for the setting up of the JSC.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: All of us are aligned in the request but not necessarily aligned in relation to the reasons for asking for the setting up of the JSC.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The hon Minister for Law chose his words very carefully in replying to me.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He said the way our service was structured "is probably the best model for the time being".

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: If anyone were to have asked me then as to whether the Government would set up the JSC, my instinctive reply would have been, "Please do not hold your breath!" Then, in July this year, hon Members Mr Christopher de Souza and Mr Lim Biow Chuan joined me in an Adjournment Motion to call on the Government to study the feasibility to set up a separate and independent JSC to allow for deeper specialisation and ensure that the Judiciary is properly positioned for the challenges of the future.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The hon Minister for Law agreed broadly with the points we made and pithily put it as an issue of timing.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The Second Minister for Law recounted this just earlier today as well.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Should we retain the current structure and make incremental changes as we go along, or should we split the services now to put our country on a better footing for the future?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: If the same person were to have repeated the question on whether the split would have happened after the Adjournment Motion, my response would likely be that I am hopeful it will happen sooner rather than later.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I am really glad to note from the hon Member Mr Dennis Tan's speech that it will enjoy bipartisan support as well.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I am highlighting this chronology as it is clear to me that the Government was already considering the merits of these changes for a while and decided that now is the time to make these changes in the interest of securing of country's future.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The Government's approach brings to my mind what Prime Minister Lee stated during his National Day Rally speech in 2016.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He asked, and I quote, "whether things could get better for Singapore after SG50.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The answer was a resounding "yes!" He went on to state that one thing we need, as a country, to ensure this is to be, and I quote, "blessed with a divine discontent, always not quite satisfied with what we have, always driven to do better".

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: These amendments we are considering reflect the spirit of "divine discontent" and "drive to do better".

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is also in keeping with the Motion on Singapore's Justice System passed in Parliament in November 2020 in which we affirmed the Government's continuous efforts to build a fair and just society.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: We should use slides that we can read.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The chart is entitled "Those who want changes to their political system are not confident political system can be changed".

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: So, you do not want to be high up in the chart from the Pew Research Center that I am showing.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Italy is ranked at the top, meaning, amongst the 17 economies, its people are the least satisfied.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Singapore is right below, meaning her people are the most satisfied.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: It is stated in the report that in every economy, except Singapore, there are larger shares of the public who want political reform but lack the confidence that reform can happen effectively as compared to those who are confident that change can occur.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: A key feature of our democracy is that real action is taken, to make changes essential to securing our future and keeping all of us united in purpose.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The significance of setting up a separate and independent JSC should not be lost on anyone in this House.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Just last month, when this House was considering the FICA Bill, there were insinuations in some quarters, particularly outside this House, that the Government is bent on making itself more powerful to suppress legitimate free speech and expression amongst our people.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: These are not the acts of a power-hungry government, hell-bent on entrenching itself and ignoring the wishes of the people.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Fair-minded people decide not based on empty words, but on real action.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The razor-sharp focus of our Government is on securing our people’s future against the backdrop of an ever more challenging global landscape.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: For the remainder of my speech, I wish to focus on the proposed reconstituted LSC.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: In my speech during the Adjournment Motion, I had spoken about the indelible contributions of the current LSC, using the integrated model since 1959, for which, as a nation, we owe much thanks.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I have also spoken about the highly-respected judicial system that we have in Singapore and how the JSC will serve to strengthen it even more under the proposed system.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: To illustrate this point, I need only ask hon Members, as the hon Second Minister for Law did just a few minutes ago, to recount their own legislative experience in this House.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Seven of these bills were urgent Bills which included the COVID-19 (Temporary Measures) Bill and its three subsequent amendment Bills, Supply Bills, Bills providing for Parliamentary elections and marriage solemnisation during COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Two hundred and twenty-seven pieces of COVID-19-related subsidiary legislation were also published.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: We were able to do this because of, amongst others, a top-rate team in the legislative division of the Attorney-General's Chambers (AGC).

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: They had to be creative but meticulous, be daring but keep an eye for the minutiae of details.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: And all is done, quoting the hon Second Minister for Law, at "breakneck speed".

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I still recall the speech of the hon Minister for Law when he expressed his pride and appreciation for the work done by officers involved during the passing of the COVID-19 (Temporary Measures) Bill.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Several hon Members, including myself, joined him to express our appreciation.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: This speaks of the quality and dedication of the officers we have in the legislative division headed by the hon Deputy Solicitor-General, Mrs Owi Beng Ki.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The Legal Branch is replete with great examples of dedicated officers, past and present, with a strong sense of duty.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: He served in the Legal Service from 1963 to 1985.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: This included a stint as the longest-serving Director of the Legal Aid Bureau, which allows people of limited means with important access to civil and family justice.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The late Mr S Tiwari, who was in the Legal Service for 36 years from 1971 to 2007 when he retired.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: During his career, he headed MINDEF's Legal Department and AGC's Civil Division and later, its International Affairs Division.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: He was involved in numerous international negotiations representing Singapore.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Mr Daren Tang, who is currently the Director-General of the World Intellectual Property Organisation (WIPO).

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: In fact, he is the first Singaporean to lead a UN Agency.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The hon Minister Mr Edwin Tong described his appointment as, and I quote, "a momentous occasion for Singapore".

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Prior to that, he was the Chief Executive of the Intellectual Property Office of Singapore and held several positions in AGC.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Mr Mohamed Faizal Senior Counsel, Senior State Counsel of the Crime Division of AGC – he is an excellent example of how one mixes heavy duty responsibilities with regular volunteer work for our community.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: For his contributions to the legal profession and the community, he was awarded the Berita Harian Anugerah Jauhari 2020 award.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: If so, I would be grateful for an outline of the efforts that will be expended on this front.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The text of the laws passed can be so turgid and formal such that many people cannot help but describe it as "gobbledegook".

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: During the pandemic, for example, these laws make sure that workers get paid, our rents reduced and that the promises businesses made to one another can be modified easily without breaking trust.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: And all these, in an orderly, legitimate and predictable manner.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: This could not have been done without the best legal minds at work in the public sector.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: This restructuring is needed, but we must do it with care.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: This will allow us to pursue our democratic dream, partnered with divine discontent, not mere dissatisfaction with the way things are, but the power to change them to the way they should be.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 4.55 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 4.32 pm until 4.55 pm.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The restructuring will allow both the LSC and JSC to benefit from greater specialisation and flexibility.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This is needed to tackle the increasing complexity of the legal landscape.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Our legal system and judiciary are greatly respected for impartially and efficiently dispensing justice.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The amendments will help us to maintain the good standing of our legal system.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have three points of clarification to make.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My first point is on the independence of the LSC, the Public Service Commission (PSC) and the JSC.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The public place great trust in our institutions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Rule of Law Index looks at, among other things, accountability and open government.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is very commendable that we have such high levels of trust locally and internationally in our public institutions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My clarification is on how we can safeguard the good reputation of our public institutions by ensuring independence of the JSC, LSC and PSC.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: There are some concerns that the proposed Articles may mean some overlap among the Commissions for the LSC, PSC and JSC.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The PSC will also advise the President on the appointment of up to two members each on the LSC and JSC.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It would be good if the Minister can share some safeguards in place to ensure the public can continue to have high confidence in the independence of the LSC, JSC and PSC.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My second point is on recruiting a wider range of talents from beyond the existing legal service into the JSC.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In July this year, my colleague Mr Murali Pillai delivered an Adjournment Motion with Mr Christopher de Souza and Mr Lim Biow Chuan on the feasibility of setting up the JSC for judicial officers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In his Motion speech, Mr Murali spoke about the flexibility the JSC may have in recruiting a wider range of talent.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: He gave the example of how someone with experience in programming who is taught law may be able to navigate the technical facts of a case much better than a legally-trained Judge.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Additionally, the three Members spoke on the benefits of the movement of judicial officers and legal service officers across judicial and legal service branches.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Such rotations are beneficial for the officers and the respective branches.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: That said, I think we can all agree that it is important for the judicial service to be staffed by officers from a diversity of backgrounds beyond the legal service.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Recruiting talent from diverse backgrounds will help with responding to increasingly complex and specialised cases before the Courts and also for maintaining trust in the judiciary’s independence.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister share the plans to diversify the talent pool of judicial officers within the JSC?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Lastly, under the new Article 111D, an appointed member to the JSC may hold office of three to five years and is eligible for reappointment.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Under the new Article 111L, an appointed member to the LSC may hold office of three to five years and is also eligible for reappointment.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Both Articles do not set out any limits for such reappointment.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Limits on reappointment are not uncommon in private and public institutions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Such limits steer institutions towards leadership renewal and organisational changes.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister confirm whether there are limits on the reappointment of any member to the LSC and JSC?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If not, can the Minister share the rationale for not limiting the number of reappointments that a member can hold in both the LSC and JSC?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: In July this year, my Parliamentary colleague, Mr Murali Pillai, filed an Adjournment Motion on the “Feasibility of Setting up a Judicial Service Commission for Judicial Officers”.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I spoke in support of the Motion as I am of the view that it is in the interest of our legal system that we have judicial officers who can be equipped to serve in the various specialised Courts and to meet the challenges of the future.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I am grateful that MinLaw supports this need to carry out structural changes to the Legal Service.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The Judiciary is one of the three Organs of State.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: It plays an integral part in upholding the rule of law and ensuring that justice is accessible to all the citizens of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: For that reason, it is important that the Government reviews the structure of the Legal Service to ensure that both judicial officers and Legal Service officers are adequately prepared for the future.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The judicial branch serves the Supreme Court, the State Court and the Family Justice Courts.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The legal branch serves the AGC and the legal service departments in various Ministries and Statutory Boards.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: As an example, the 582 LSOs serve in Government agencies other than AGC, like they serve in ACRA, the Competition and Consumer Commission of Singapore (CCCS), EDB, Health Service Authority (HSA), IMDA, IPOS, IRAS, Office of Public Guardian (OPG), LTA, SLA, NEA, SMC, MUIS and so on.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: So, it is really a wide scope for these LSOs.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The caseload for the State Courts for 2019 was higher at 249,954 cases.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The caseload for 2018 was even higher at 359,064 cases.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Then we go on to the Family Justice Courts.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The caseload is 25,633 cases for 2020 and 27,953 cases for 2019.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: If you add the total caseloads of the State Courts, the Family Justice Courts and the work in the Supreme Court, many of us will agree that the 224 judicial officers, even with support staff, will be grossly overstretched.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The Singapore Courts Annual Report also gave examples of significant cases handled by the Courts.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: There was a case about terrorism financing, a case about defamatory comments made on social media against an F&B company; there are cases about protection to be given to litigants under the Prevention of Harassment Act and even a case about euthanasia of a dog.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: In a 2020 case involving cryptocurrency, the Court had to make a decision involving cryptocurrency trades and the implications of smart contracts and artificial intelligence.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: In the not too far future, judges may be called upon to decide who is at fault if there are accidents involving driverless cars.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Another example of the evolving law is in the area of family law.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: In the past, lawyers acting for parties who have filed for divorce would work towards getting the best resolution for their clients.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: And that is the nature of an adversarial system.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Today, lawyers and judges alike, would have to adjust to this concept of therapeutic justice in family disputes.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Based on the volume of cases handled by the State Courts and Family Justice Courts and the increasing complexity of cases, I would submit that it is timely for us to review the need for our judicial officers to have greater specialisation so as to gain greater depth of knowledge about the latest developments in the law.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: There has always been a high regard for our judicial system.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The Singapore judiciary and our legal system have always been recognised as among the best in the world.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Within Singapore, a recent survey by the Institute of Policy Studies shows that 82% of the respondents had either a great deal or quite a lot of trust in our Courts.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Minister Indranee Rajah had said in her 2014 speech on the Subordinate Courts (Amendment) Bill, “the public reposes a great deal of trust and confidence in the Subordinate Courts – and, indeed, our Judiciary generally.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: We trust them to apply the law impartially, uphold our laws and dispense justice fairly.” Our Chief Justice said recently society’s regard for and trust in the Courts are “extremely precious”.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: For that reason, Sir, I submit that we need to invest heavily in our legal officers serving both in the Judiciary as well as in the Legal Service so that we can continue to earn and maintain the trust of the people in our legal system.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Having a separate Judicial Service Commission and a Legal Service Commission is just a step towards recognising the challenges facing our LSOs and allow them to explore greater specialisation and more equipped for the future.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Having a personnel board for each commission also ensures that we continue to attract and retain talent to serve in the legal and judicial services.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Our judicial officers need more specialised knowledge to better grasp the complex laws and facts; they also need equipping to understand the different emotions of the litigant.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: And that is not an easy task for Judicial officers.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I quote Lord Judge, the former Lord Chief Justice in the UK, in a speech which he made in October 2008.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: He said, “Many qualities are required of a judge… He or she must, of course, know the law, and know how to apply it, but the judge must always be wise to the ways of the world.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The judge must have the ability to make a decision." "Decisions can be profoundly unpleasant.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: For example, to say to a mother that her children would be taken away from her, or to say to an individual that he is going to prison for the rest of his life." "Judges must have moral courage.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: It is an important judicial attribute to make decisions that will be unpopular with the politicians or the media and the public, and, indeed, perhaps, most importantly of all, to defend the right to equal treatment before the law, of those who are unpopular at any given time.” So, even the person who may be very unpopular or condemned by social media or members of the public, it is the job of a judge to ensure that this person is given the right to equal treatment before the law, even if they are unpopular at any point of time.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: These are wise words because judicial officers would need to deal firmly with recalcitrant offenders and yet show compassion to an accused person who may have made a mistake due to poor judgement or reacted badly due to a breakdown in emotions.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: That judicial officer would then be armed with practical life skills that would make him or her a better judge in the Family Justice Courts.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: These functions were previously carried out by the Legal Services Commission, which oversaw all legal officers in the Public Service, including both the judicial services, those in the Attorney-General’s Chambers and those in other public agencies.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The Legal Services Commission will remain, but its remit will no longer cover judicial officers.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The rationale for such changes is that it allows specialisation in each of the services and for the senior officers in each branch to properly evaluate and appoint the officers to that branch.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: There is also an argument that this provides a cleaner separation of powers, with judicial officers cleanly separated from those performing other functions, such as in public prosecution.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This separation of functions exists in many countries, including many in the Commonwealth.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Having said that, this matter has been raised before, including in this House, and in the past, we had always believed that having a single Legal Services Commission had worked well for Singapore and had certain advantages.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This included that officers could be rotated across functions and to develop broader experiences.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Judicial officers, for example, could benefit from having had stints as counsel, such as public prosecutors.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Similarly, those acting as public prosecutors may also benefit from having spent time as registrars, or even as district judges, as they will see matters from the perspective of the bench.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Is there also a risk that if an officer stays only in one branch of the service, they may not get the broader perspective they used to be able to get in the past that will help them perform their functions better?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Does this also mean that legal careers will be set in stone, depending on which side of the branch they start in?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim asked about the definition of “subordinate court” as used in clause 26 of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As set out in clause 26, on the appointed date, the existing Judicial Branch officers will be assigned to the Judicial Service, and all other Legal Service officers will remain in the reconstituted Legal Service.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: A Judicial Branch officer is defined as an officer holding a post in the Supreme Court or a subordinate court immediately before the date of the commencement of the Act.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: To avoid doubt, the LSC Secretariat will be notifying the individual officers of the Service that they have been assigned to.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Louis Ng asked about the safeguards for judicial independence, notwithstanding the "overlaps" in the composition of the JSC, LSC and PSC.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I think he refers to the overlap in question, which is the Chairman of PSC.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: On Chairman/PSC's presence on both the JSC and LSC, Mr Louis Ng might be interested to know that, in fact, the 1959 Constitution, which I referred to earlier and which first established the LSC, already provided for the Chairman of PSC to be an ex-officio member of the LSC and that, has since, remained unchanged.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, we are simply using that and Chairman/PSC remains now on both of the two Commissions, post-split.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It has allowed the LSC to draw from the best practices, particularly from a human resource perspective, of the PSC, while the Commissions remain separate and independent.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The JSC and the LSC can draw on Chairman/PSC's experience and expertise whilst the various Commissions remain separate and independent.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: There is no question of Chairman/PSC's ability to act independently.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: He is himself appointed by the President in her discretion, acting on the advice of the Prime Minister, and there are constitutional safeguards, which I have outlined earlier, to secure his independence.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Louis Ng also mentioned that Chairman/PSC nominates up to two members each on the JSC and the LSC.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Again, as I have said in my opening speech, this is something that has already been in place since the 1959 Constitution although, prior to 2007, Chairman/PSC could nominate two members of the PSC directly to the LSC, whereas, today, Chairman/PSC advises the President on the appointment of up to two members and the President has the discretion to veto such nominations.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In fact, just to be complete, this is on the same footing as the Chief Justice and the Prime Minister.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Their nominees are also subject to the President's veto.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Even if, for the sake of argument, one were to accept that there is some risk that Chairman/PSC would not act independently, this concern is premised on the notion that Chairman/PSC's nominees will somehow be unable to act independently as well.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But Mr Louis Ng will be assured to know that the appointments of both JSC and LSC members, including the Chairman of PSC's nominees, will be made by the President, acting in her discretion.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: She discharges her duties with a direct mandate from the electorate.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The eligibility criteria for JSC and LSC members are also set out in the Constitution and designed to make sure that members have no formal political links.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Just for Members' information, Article 111K sets out the qualifications, and 111L sets out the disqualifications.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In addition, all JSC and LSC members must take an oath of office and it will be an offence for any member to disclose any information in connection with any matter referred to the Commission.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Louis Ng asked if there are limits on the reappointment of JSC and LSC members and, if not, the reasons for not limiting the number of reappointments that a member can hold on the JSC and LSC.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Whilst we understand Mr Louis Ng's concerns about leadership renewal and organisational change, we must also, at the same time, be realistic about the pool of candidates that are suitable and also willing to serve on these Commissions.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Candidates must be suitably qualified – I set out earlier the Articles that prescribe the criteria – and sufficiently senior, with experience, and for those from the private sector especially, must be willing to devote time and energy to Public Service.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We want the best people to sit on both Commissions.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Given our small size, this pool is not large.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It is not feasible to impose strict limits on reappointments, which would not lead to the best results for both Commissions.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Next, let me touch on secondments and transfers.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Both Mr Lim Biow Chuan and Mr Vikram Nair spoke on the benefits of secondments in providing breadth of exposure for officers.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Lim asked for confirmation that such secondments would continue.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Nair asked if secondments would be more difficult after the restructuring since there are different Commissions governing the officers and whether there is a risk that if an officer remains in one Branch, they would not get a broader perspective that will help them to perform their functions better.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In the same vein, Mr Zhulkarnain made a number of proposals on secondments for exposure.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Zhulkarnain, in particular, asked if permanent transfers will be available where necessary to meet manpower needs and if the possibility for suitable Judicial Officers (JOs) to be seconded to the Syariah Court can be retained.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I welcome Mr Lim's, Mr Nair's and Mr Zhulkarnain's points.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The goal of the restructuring is to better support the training and development of officers in the Judicial Service and the Legal Service.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We want to provide the best development opportunities for officers.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As I mentioned in my opening speech, both the Judicial and Legal Branches have now matured to a state where there are diverse opportunities within each Branch – not just across but within each Branch – for exposure.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Nevertheless, as I have mentioned earlier, secondments will continue to be made available under a framework to be discussed and agreed upon by both Commissions.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: With the restructuring, I expect that the two Commissions will explore even more innovative ways of enhancing the development of both Legal and Judicial Service Officers.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In this regard, I am sure that the Commissions will take very seriously the various proposals and suggestions that Members have put forward.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Pillai and Mr Ng touched on talent attraction and talent diversification in their speeches respectively.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Pillai asked how the reconstituted LSC plans to attract and retain its fair share of top talent with the right set of values after restructuring.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Those are perennial problems, not just today, previously but also in the private sector.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Louis Ng queried if there are plans to diversify the talent pool of judicial officers within the JSC.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: First, let me thank Mr Pillai's impassioned speech and his recognition of the impactful work undertaken by the LSOs in the past year and a half, at least.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It has been a challenging period – as Mr Pillai illustrated with various examples – but the officers, I think we can agree, have delivered far beyond expectations.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The plans going forward are matters for the new Commissions when they are constituted.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: That is precisely why they are set up with the respective Personnel Boards.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Nevertheless, I am sure that both the Chief Justice and the Attorney-General, as the future Presidents of the two Commissions, share Mr Pillai's concerns that both their Services must continue to attract the right legal talent with a heart for service and a care for Singapore in their respective domains.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: That would not be compatible with the spirit of the amendments that we are proposing.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The issue of talent diversification – I have to come back to this point that I think Mr Louis Ng also raised – and, more importantly, ensuring that we have the right people with the relevant skillsets and also temperament for the Bench will, undoubtedly, be on the forefront of the minds of the JSC.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I had earlier mentioned in my speech how both the Judicial and Legal Branches have been taking measures to deepen specialisation within their own skillsets.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They will continue to build on these efforts after the restructuring.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: With the restructuring, the two Commissions will have the flexibility to also develop their own unique value proposition in terms of breadth of exposure for their officers, talent development, opportunities for career progression, recruitment and so on.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As I have said earlier, the competition is not just within the Service.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It is how do we attract the best talent, given that we have developed the legal industry, the legal landscape in Singapore to an extent where the top talent does exist in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But I am confident that the two Commissions will be able to chart the way forward for the respective Services as we enter this next stage of institution-building.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: On this note, Mr Dennis Tan asked about caseloads.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Lim Biow Chuan also cited some figures.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, they are progressively clearing a backlog and making sure that cases are disposed of more expeditiously.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I cannot speak for their manpower needs moving forward but, certainly, this demonstrates that officers have been working hard to ensure that justice is not just served correctly but served expeditiously as well.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Zhulkarnain mentioned ensuring opportunities for cross-learning between the two Services and that the Singapore Judicial College could be involved.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We agree that the Services must continue sharing knowledge and best practices even after the restructuring, and we will pass this feedback on to the two Commissions.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Dennis Tan asked about career development after the split of the two Commissions.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But I can say to Mr Tan that their focus will be what works best for Singapore, how best to attract and retain talent and how best to develop their respective officers, as I have mentioned earlier.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Members might also wish to know that after the Adjournment Motion by Mr Pillai, there were townhalls held by the Working Group.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I have touched on, I think, almost all of the queries.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I had raised attention to the good work of the Legislation Division of the Attorney-General's Chambers, headed by Mrs Owi, the Deputy Solicitor-General.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: It is my hope that this service of excellence will reach even greater heights under the reconstituted LSC.
